# Your Startup Needs a GTM Strategy, Not Just a List of Tactics

Source: https://lowob.com/research/gtm-strategy-vs-tactics/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-04-25 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A list of channels and campaigns is not a go-to-market strategy. A strategy makes four connected decisions (market, message, motion and measurement) and every tactic then has a specific job inside them. This playbook sets out the decisions, a coherence test and seven questions to answer before approving another campaign.

A go-to-market plan connects the right buyer, a useful promise, a credible channel and measurable customer behavior. Most startup plans are lists of tactics instead: launch the site, hire a seller, post, sponsor, build a Discord. A tactic answers what the team will do. A strategy answers why these actions should create an advantage for this company, with this customer, at this moment. The test is coherence: four decisions on market, message, motion and measurement that reinforce one another.

Most startup go-to-market plans look reassuring in a slide deck.

Launch the website. Hire a salesperson. Post on LinkedIn. Start a newsletter. Sponsor a conference. Build a Discord. Run paid media. Recruit creators. Announce partnerships.

None of those decisions is necessarily wrong. Together, however, they still do not constitute a strategy.

A tactic answers: **What are we going to do?**

A strategy answers: **Why should these actions create an advantage for this particular company, with this particular customer, at this particular moment?**

That distinction matters because activity is easy to manufacture. A small team can fill a calendar for months without learning whether anyone has a painful problem, whether the product solves it, or whether the company can reach the buyer economically. A busy launch can disguise a missing commercial thesis.

## Why a list is not a strategy

The strategy literature has made this point for decades. Michael Porter's "What Is Strategy?" in *Harvard Business Review* (1996) separated operational effectiveness from strategy: "Improving operational effectiveness is a necessary part of management, but it is not strategy." He defined strategy as "creating fit among a company's activities" and wrote that "the essence of strategy is choosing what not to do." A tactic list fails both tests. It does not choose, and its items are not designed to fit.

Richard Rumelt made a similar argument in a 2007 *McKinsey Quarterly* interview: "Most corporate strategic plans have little to do with strategy." He described much of what executives called strategy as resource budgets and market share projections, and coined "doorknob polishing" for initiatives with no clear position behind them. A startup's launch calendar is the small-company version of the same thing.

The commercial cost shows up in the buyer. Forrester's State of Business Buying 2024 found an average of 13 people involved in a purchase decision, with 89% of purchases spanning two or more departments. Gartner's survey of 632 buyers, published in May 2025, found 74% of buyer teams showed unhealthy conflict during the decision, and groups that reached consensus were 2.5 times more likely to report a high-quality deal. Tactics aimed at one person in that group, with no view on the others, create meetings that do not become decisions.

## The four decisions hiding underneath GTM

A credible GTM strategy makes four connected decisions. They are the same four decisions set out in [What go-to-market means](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-gtm-for-founders/), stated here as strategic choices.

**Market:** Which narrowly defined group has the strongest combination of pain, urgency, authority, and ability to pay?

"Fintech companies" is not a market. "U.S. consumer fintech companies preparing to launch an embedded stablecoin product in the next two quarters" might be. The second definition gives the team observable signals, relevant decision-makers, and a reason the conversation matters now.

**Message:** What must the buyer believe before taking the next step?

Early-stage teams tend to describe the product. Buyers evaluate a change. They want to know what improves, what risk disappears, why the timing matters, and why this team is credible. Good messaging translates technical capability into a change the buyer can recognize.

**Motion:** How will trust move from zero to a commercial decision?

A self-serve product, an enterprise sale, an ecosystem partnership, and a developer platform do not share the same buying journey. The motion determines whether the primary engine should be product-led onboarding, founder-led sales, channel partnerships, community adoption, or a carefully sequenced combination. [Product-led vs sales-led vs partner-led growth](https://lowob.com/research/product-led-vs-sales-led-vs-partner-led/) compares them.

**Measurement:** What evidence will tell the team that the thesis is working?

Impressions and followers can be useful leading indicators, but they are not automatically commercial evidence. A good measurement system connects attention to qualified conversations, product behavior, pipeline progression, retention, and revenue.

## The GTM coherence test

Write one sentence for each of the four decisions. Then ask whether they reinforce one another.

| If the market is... | ...and the motion or measure is... | The incoherence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Risk-conscious institutional buyers | Viral social content and an anonymous Discord | The channel cannot carry the trust the buyer needs |
| A developer community | Executive sales meetings as the only measure | The evidence is being looked for in the wrong place |
| Not urgent | Ever more refined messaging | No message creates a buying event that does not exist |
| A 13-person buying group | Outreach to one champion only | The deal stalls at the people nobody wrote for |

A coherent example sounds more like this, illustrative and unnamed:

*We help regional financial institutions preparing stablecoin products reduce the time and operational uncertainty involved in evaluating infrastructure partners. We reach the executive sponsor through research-led account outreach and industry relationships, then support technical validation with a structured diligence process. We measure qualified evaluations, stakeholder expansion, technical milestones, and time to commercial decision.*

That is not a slogan. It is a theory of how a market turns into revenue.

> A busy launch can disguise a missing commercial thesis.

## Build the strategy before filling the calendar

Before approving another campaign, force the team to answer seven questions. Each maps to one of the four decisions and has a place to find the answer.

| Question | Decision | Where the evidence usually is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Which customer has the most expensive version of the problem? | Market | Won deals, deal size and retention by segment |
| 2. What event makes solving it urgent now? | Market | Discovery notes; the trigger behind the last five wins |
| 3. Who feels the problem, who approves the change, and who can block it? | Motion | Contacts on won and lost deals |
| 4. What alternative is the buyer using today? | Message | Win-loss interviews; "what would you do without us" |
| 5. What must the buyer believe to move forward? | Message | Objections recorded in calls |
| 6. Which channel can transfer enough trust to earn the next step? | Motion | Source of each customer, and what it cost |
| 7. What observable behavior would prove the thesis is working? | Measurement | The one weekly number the team agrees on |

Only after those answers are clear should the team select channels, content, events, partners, and campaign tactics. Each tactic then gets a job written against one of the four decisions. Our piece [The commercial system: what it is](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-system-what-it-is/) describes how those decisions are recorded so the team keeps them, and [Positioning for complex markets](https://lowob.com/research/positioning-for-complex-markets/) covers questions 4 and 5 in depth.

## The uncomfortable conclusion

Many companies do not have a marketing problem or a sales problem. They have a coherence problem. The priority customer, narrative, distribution model, and evidence system were designed separately, or never designed at all.

**The solution is not another tactic. It is a commercial system in which every tactic has a specific job.**

Illustrative example: cutting the calendar to fit the thesis

Decision
:   Stop three planned tactics (a general conference sponsorship, a community launch and paid social) and fund research-led outreach to 40 named institutions plus a structured technical diligence pack.

Reason and owner
:   The coherence test showed the market was risk-conscious institutions, while two-thirds of the planned spend went to channels those buyers did not use to evaluate suppliers. Owned by the CEO, with the head of growth.

What changed
:   The team measured qualified evaluations and stakeholders engaged per account instead of impressions, and could say which activity produced each evaluation.

Illustrative: a composite of an early-stage infrastructure company, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Choose the buyer and problem before picking channels.** Market is the first decision, and it constrains the other three.
- **Test for coherence.** Write one sentence per decision and check the motion can carry the trust this buyer needs.
- **Give every campaign a job.** Each tactic should trace to one of the four decisions and to a commercial outcome.
- **Stop funding activity that cannot show why it matters.** Choosing what not to do is the strategy.

Take your current GTM plan and label every tactic with the one decision it serves: market, message, motion or measurement. Pause any tactic that cannot be labelled, and write the seven answers before funding it again.
